summary.text: Sparta was a prominent ancient Greek polis in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese, and the state itself was known in classical antiquity as Lacedaemon.
Its society was exceptionally militarised: citizens called Spartiates focused on military training and were legally barred from productive economic activity.
It rose in the 7th century BC to become the most prominent land military power in the Greek world, a status it kept until its defeat at Leuctra in 371 BC.

facts.label: Helot share
facts.value: Helots made up the vast majority of the population

facts.label: Training regimen
facts.value: Spartiate men underwent the harsh agoge

facts.label: Supposed lawgiver
facts.value: The semi-mythical Lycurgus introduced its system

facts.label: Defeat at Leuctra
facts.value: Epaminondas beat Sparta there in 371 BC

items.prompt: After a victory by Epaminondas at Leuctra, Sparta lost control of a region it had ruled. Why did that send it into decline as a military power?

options.label: The region's soldiers began fighting for Thebes
It lost the slave labour that region provided
It lost its only port on the sea
It lost the region's silver mines

items.explain: Messenia was freed from Spartan rule, and the loss of the slave labour it provided sent Sparta into terminal decline as a military power.

items.prompt: A Spartiate man trains for war from youth and is legally barred from productive economic work. What does this show about Sparta?

options.label: Its citizens were farmers called up only in wartime
Its economy was run by wealthy citizen merchants
Its men trained but could freely choose any trade
Its citizen class was devoted entirely to military life

items.explain: Spartan society was exceptionally militarised, focusing the Spartiate class on training and legally barring them from productive economic activity.

items.prompt: Most people in Sparta were state-owned helots, treated exceptionally harshly, including by the Crypteia. What did this lead to?

options.label: Repeated uprisings by the helots
Helots earning citizenship through military service
Helots becoming the ruling class
A shrinking helot population as many moved to Athens

items.explain: Helots suffered exceptionally harsh treatment, which caused repeated revolts, and social mobility was nearly nonexistent.

items.prompt: One ancient writer calls a place Sparta and another calls it Lacedaemon. What is the usual difference?

options.label: Sparta was the state or region; Lacedaemon was the capital
They named two rival cities that later merged
Sparta was the capital's villages; Lacedaemon was the state or region
Only Roman writers ever used the name Lacedaemon

items.explain: Sparta referred to the main cluster of settlements, while Lacedaemon named the state and typically the region.

items.prompt: Ancient Sparta sat on the banks of Laconia's largest river, in a valley that worked as a natural fortress. What did that river give the city?

options.label: A harbour for its warships
A source of fresh water
A trade route to Athens
Fertile fields for its allies

items.explain: The Eurotas, the largest river of Laconia, provided Sparta with a source of fresh water, and its valley was a natural fortress.

items.prompt: In the Peloponnesian War, Sparta led an alliance against the Athenian Empire. How did it end for the Spartan side?

options.label: It lost, after Athens won a naval battle at Aegospotami
It ended in a draw when both sides signed a treaty
It won, after Leonidas held the pass at Thermopylae
It won, after Lysander's naval victory at Aegospotami

items.explain: Sparta led the Peloponnesian League against Athens and emerged victorious after Lysander's naval victory at Aegospotami.
